newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian Socialists oppose wider cabinet powers.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian Socialists oppose wider cabinet powers.

text.p: Bulgaria's Socialist rulers, apparently determined not to leave power quietly, say they will vote against giving a caretaker cabinet powers to seek grain credits and negotiate with the International Monetary Fund.

President Petar Stoyanov, who last week brokered an agreement ending a month of street protests against Socialist rule, will name a caretaker cabinet this week to govern the crisis-stricken country until elections in mid-April.

The Socialists boycotted parliament on Thursday and Friday but say they will return for next week's session to discuss amendments to the income tax law and the electoral law, and a bill giving the caretaker government a mandate to borrow funds for grain imports and negotiate new funds from the IMF.

National television quoted party leader Georgi Parvanov as saying on Saturday in the southeastern town of Kardzhali that they would not support extra powers for the caretaker cabinet, which is strictly only empowered to organise the elections.
The Socialists are deeply divided and it is not clear how many deputies will toe the party line.
The IMF had said it was ready to send a mission as soon as a cabinet was in place to resume talks on new funding to avert default on Bulgaria's foreign debt.
The national currency has been in free fall since the beginning of the year, and inflation is put at 50 percent for January alone.
On Thursday, the cabinet doubled state salaries and the minimum wage is now 11,000 levs, or about $3.60. Democratsiya daily said pensioners in the town of Plovdiv were trapping pigeons for food.
Many petrol stations are without fuel, and the Sofia public transport authority has warned it may halt services on Tuesday if it does not get more diesel.
The Neftohim oil refinery, which has no money to import crude, said on Saturday it was operating at its critical minimum.
"This is now a country which politicians in eastern Europe use to threaten their voters with," the Troud daily said on Sunday.

The caretaker cabinet, expected to be led by Sofia's respected mayor Stefan Sofianski, will take office once parliament has cleared outstanding business. A session is scheduled for Tuesday or Wednesday.

"With the price of bread about to be 1,000 levs, it will not be surprising if we have tuberculosis in our country, something we have not experienced for years," said the Standart daily in an editorial.
"The health experiments of (Health Minister) Mimi Vitkova have led the nation to the point where a simple flu attack can kill because people have no money to buy food or medecine."

The IMF last year proposed a strict fixed exchange rate regime matching levs in circulation to central bank reserves, as a last resort to restore confidence and halt hyper-inflation by preventing the government from printing money.
The new parliament would have to vote the necessary legislation, but the IMF had planned to send a mission to prepare implementation measures with the interim cabinet.
Representatives of three polling agencies interviewed by Darik radio said that, if polls were held now, the opposition would win two thirds of the vote and the Socialists 15 percent.
But they said defections of prominent reformists to a new Euro-Left movement could split the vote to eight percent for the Bulgarian Socialist Party and seven for the Euro-Left.
